obtained.how: Alaska Resources Library & Information Services (ARLIS) scan of the USFWS report, with a text layer

bibliography.checked_against: the report's title page and its 'should be cited as' line
bibliography.note: 'Allen, A. W. 1984. Habitat suitability index models: Mink. U.S. Fish Wildl. Serv. FWS/OBS-82/10.61 Revised. 19 pp.'; title page 'FWS/OBS-82/10.61 Revised, May 1984'. Matches. The entry's 'first issued 1983' is not stated in this copy (only that this is a revision).

claims.source_value: chiefly nocturnal and active throughout the year (Marshall 1936; Gerell 1969; Burgess 1978)
claims.location: p. 1 (PDF p. 9), Habitat use information, General
claims.quote: Mink are chiefly nocturnal and remain active throughout the year

claims.claim: They eat fish in winter and spring, crayfish in summer and small mammals in autumn
claims.source_value: fish are preferentially eaten in winter and spring (Sweden, Gerell 1969); crayfish commonest in summer (Sweden, Gerell 1967; Quebec, Burgess 1978); small terrestrial mammals increasingly important with the approach of fall (Gerell 1967, 1969; Burgess 1978)
claims.quote: Fish are preferentially consumed in winter and spring due to their increased vulnerability
claims.conditions: literature review; the seasonal pattern is from Swedish and Quebec studies; Allen stresses that diet varies with season, prey availability and habitat (birds dominated in North Dakota prairie marshes, muskrats in Ontario)
claims.note: Allen gives the fish season's reason as low water levels and low temperatures making fish vulnerable.

claims.claim: they typically work no more than about 300 m of shore a day
claims.source_value: during daily activity periods mink move back and forth in a core area that typically does not exceed 300 m of shoreline (Gerell 1970), later shifting to another den and core area
claims.quote: typically does not exceed 300 m (984 ft) in shoreline length
claims.note: It is the length of the daily core area, not a measured daily travel distance; the home range is larger (several core areas).

claims.claim: and reached densities of 1.5 to over 3 per km of shore on the Vancouver Island coast (Allen 1984)
claims.source_value: 1.5 to more than 3 animals per km of shoreline along the coast of Vancouver Island (Hatler 1976)
claims.quote: Vancouver Island ranged from 1.5 to more than 3 animals/km
claims.conditions: marine coast, British Columbia (Hatler 1976), via Allen's review
claims.note: A marine-shore density; Allen also notes that coastal food supply year-round gives higher mink densities, so it may overstate a lake shore.

notes: Other values in the review: in Idaho mink were believed able to sustain themselves in a 1–2 km section of stream; female home ranges 7.7 ha in dense cover against 20.1 ha on grazed shore (Montana), under 8 ha in Michigan; most Quebec activity within 3 m of stream edges; dens 5–100 m from water in Idaho. All secondary to the studies Allen cites.
